clue.text: Fellow abridged short pieces of writing

indicators.note: an abridged text has been cut short, so the following word loses its final letter

parts.note: a chap is a man or fellow
terse means short or curt

explanation.surface: A man has cut down some brief written pieces, like an editor trimming essays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abridged' looks like it describes the writing, but it trims the word for short instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Chapters are the sections a book is divided into, each a piece of writing in its own right.

clue.text: Company knowledgable about way of obtaining discount?

parts.note: standard abbreviation for company
to be up on a subject is to be well informed about it

explanation.surface: A firm that knows the tricks for getting money off.
explanation.definitionFit: A coupon is a voucher handed over to get a reduced price, one way to secure a discount.

clue.text: Wonder about brief high point for some time

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first word goes round the other piece

parts.note: awe is a feeling of wonder

indicators.note: brief means cut short, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a hill is a raised point of land

explanation.surface: Someone marvels at a short-lived peak that lasts a while.
explanation.definitionFit: Awhile is an adverb meaning for a short period, which is for some time.

clue.text: Silenced and told the heartless rat off

indicators.note: heartless means without the heart, so the middle letter of the word is removed
off means gone wrong or bad, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
rat without its middle letter

explanation.surface: Someone shut up and was told the cruel rat had gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Told the rat off' reads as a scolding; 'off' is in fact the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To throttle someone is to choke them, and figuratively to suppress or silence them.

clue.text: Lead actor upset about new passionate speeches

indicators.note: upset means turned upside down, which in a down clue reads the word from bottom to top
about means surrounding, so the turned word goes round the other piece

parts.note: the star is the leading performer
standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A troubled leading man fumes about a fresh round of impassioned speeches.
explanation.definitionFit: Rants are long, loud, angry speeches, which are passionate in tone.

clue.text: British university expresses revolutionary argument

parts.note: standard abbreviation for British
standard abbreviation for university

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns right over, so this word is read from its end back to its start

parts.note: to put something is to express it in words

explanation.surface: A British university voices radical opinions, as student politics tends to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' seems to describe the university's politics, but it turns the word for expresses round.
explanation.definitionFit: A bust-up is an informal British term for a noisy quarrel or row.

clue.text: Useful item worth little in board game?

definitions.text: item worth little in board game?
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read as two words: a Scrabble tile bearing a vowel that scores only one point

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as U TILE: in Scrabble the U tile is worth just one point, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Utile is a formal or archaic adjective for useful, from the French and Latin for practical.

clue.text: Drunk full of endless hogwash in final years

indicators.note: full of means filled with, so the word for drunk takes the other piece inside

parts.note: tight is informal for drunk

indicators.note: endless means with both ends gone, so only the middle letters of the word are kept

parts.note: the inner letters of swill, pig food, which hogwash literally is

explanation.surface: A drunk spouting endless nonsense in later life.
explanation.walkthrough: Hogwash means nonsense, but its literal sense is pig swill, which is the word cut here.
explanation.definitionFit: Twilight is the dim end of the day, used figuratively for the closing period of a life or career.

clue.text: Character almost went astray in The Borders?

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: an actor's part is the character played
to err is to go astray

explanation.surface: A character nearly lost his way in the Scottish Borders region.
explanation.walkthrough: The Borders is a region of southern Scotland; the question mark reinterprets it as flower borders, as in a formal garden.
explanation.definitionFit: A parterre is a formal garden of ornamental flower beds and borders laid out in a pattern.

clue.text: Guiding American group around empty house

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the American group's words sit either side of the other piece

parts.note: abbreviation for the United States

indicators.note: an empty word has had its inside cleared out, leaving only its first and last letters

parts.note: the outside letters of house
a ring is a group or circle of people

explanation.surface: A band of Americans tours an abandoned house, as on a ghost-hunting trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The American group is split in two so that it surrounds the emptied house, one part each side.
explanation.definitionFit: Ushering means showing someone the way, leading or escorting them, which is guiding.

clue.text: Comic that is beginning to ridicule councillor

parts.note: Viz is a long-running British adult humour comic magazine
i.e. is the abbreviation for id est, that is

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of ridicule

explanation.surface: A satirical magazine starts mocking a local councillor.
explanation.walkthrough: Viz is a crude British comic magazine, which makes the mockery of a councillor plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: A vizier was a high official or counsellor to a Muslim ruler, an adviser of state.

clue.text: Brief week in bed

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the word that follows it

parts.note: a bed is a layer, as of rock or sediment
standard abbreviation for week

explanation.surface: A short week spent lying in bed, perhaps with illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief' looks like an adjective for the week; it is a noun, slang for a barrister.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a brief is a lawyer, especially one defending a client in court.

clue.text: Show letters implicating junior member of parliament

indicators.note: to implicate is to involve or contain, so the run of letters is held within these words

parts.note: found spanning the two words

explanation.surface: Revealed correspondence incriminates a backbench MP in a political scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: A group of owls is called a parliament, so a young bird is a junior member of one.
explanation.definitionFit: An owlet is a young owl, and the collective noun for owls is a parliament.

clue.text: Announce team in America

parts.note: to state is to announce or declare
a side is a sports team

explanation.surface: A sports club reveals its line-up during a tour of the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Stateside is an informal adverb meaning in or towards the United States.

clue.text: Game play outwardly involves chance

indicators.note: to involve is to wrap in, so one piece is enclosed by the other
outwardly points to the outside of the word, so only its two end letters remain

parts.note: the outside letters of play
luck is chance or fortune

explanation.surface: A game of play that depends on luck, like a card game or dice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like a noun introducing a sport, but here it is the adjective meaning willing and brave.
explanation.definitionFit: Game as an adjective means ready and spirited, which is to say brave or courageous.

clue.text: Conservative fool lives for drink

parts.note: standard abbreviation for Conservative
an ass is a fool
to be is to exist or live

explanation.surface: A Tory idiot exists only for the bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassis is a blackcurrant liqueur, a drink often added to white wine to make kir.

clue.text: Detest crime that involves injuring men

parts.note: actual bodily harm, a British criminal offence of assault causing injury
other ranks: soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Someone loathes violent offences that hurt men.
explanation.walkthrough: ABH, actual bodily harm, is an assault charge in English law; 'men' as OR is a military convention.
explanation.definitionFit: To abhor something is to regard it with loathing, a strong synonym of detest.

clue.text: Dislike suggestion that abruptly upset some hosts

indicators.note: a host takes guests in, so the last word wraps round the jumbled letters
upset means thrown into disorder, so these letters are mixed up
abruptly means cut off suddenly, so the word stops short of its last letter

parts.note: taken as written
any can mean some, as in 'have you any?'
a tip is a hint or suggestion

explanation.surface: Antipathy arises when a curt remark offends a number of hosts.
explanation.walkthrough: The scrambled letters sit between the N and Y of the host word.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipathy is a deep-seated aversion, which is a strong form of dislike.

clue.text: Places one goes to play and bathe at respectable houses

indicators.note: to house something is to contain it, so the answer sits inside these words

parts.note: found running across the three words

explanation.surface: Where you go to have fun and to bathe, at decent establishments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' suggests leisure, but here it is a stage play.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatres are buildings where people go to watch a play being performed.

clue.text: Barrier that hurt introduction of electric vehicle

parts.note: a bar is a barrier
ouch is what you say when something hurts

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is used

parts.note: the opening letter of electric

explanation.surface: A barrier painfully halted the launch of an electric car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Electric vehicle' suggests a modern car; the answer is the opposite, drawn by horses.
explanation.definitionFit: A barouche is a four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with a folding hood, a type of vehicle.

clue.text: Firm keeping nothing in store

indicators.note: keeping means holding something within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: firm means solid or hard
nothing is zero, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A company holds no stock in its shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' and 'store' suggest a business, but firm is the adjective, and store the noun for a stockpile.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoard is a stash or stockpile of something put by, which is a store.

clue.text: Guarantor undoubtedly voided treaty

parts.note: sure means certainly, without doubt

indicators.note: something voided has been emptied, so only the outside letters of the word are left

parts.note: the outside letters of treaty

explanation.surface: A treaty has definitely been annulled, leaving its backers exposed.
explanation.definitionFit: A surety is a person who takes responsibility for another's debt or obligation, a guarantor.

clue.text: Like cast's second attempt for the audience

indicators.note: an audience hears rather than reads, so the words are to be taken by their sound

parts.note: in filming, the second shot of a scene is take two

explanation.surface: The actors enjoyed their second attempt at a scene, performed before spectators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' is the verb, as in to come to like someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To take to someone is to begin to like them, so the phrase is a verbal synonym.

clue.text: Timeless act or rock god?

indicators.note: timeless means without time, whose abbreviation is removed from the word

parts.note: a statute is an act of parliament

explanation.surface: An enduring performance from a rock star idolised as a god.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock god' suggests a guitar hero; the question mark reinterprets it as a deity carved from stone.
explanation.definitionFit: A statue of a deity sculpted in stone is literally a god made of rock.

clue.text: High regard for each helping to host party

indicators.note: a host has guests inside, so the preceding words wrap round the party

parts.note: a as in 'two pounds a head', meaning per
a do is a party or social event
a ration is an allotted helping

explanation.surface: Respect shown to each person who helps to throw a party.
explanation.walkthrough: A and RATION together are the host, with the party sitting between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Adoration is deep love and respect, which is very high regard.

clue.text: Came up behind nurses beginning to operate

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, so the first word cradles the other piece

parts.note: arse is British slang for the backside

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, the only one kept

parts.note: the first letter of operate

explanation.surface: Something emerged from the rear as nurses started to operate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' looks like a preposition but is the noun for the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Arose is the past tense of arise, meaning rose up or came up.

clue.text: Famous philanthropist from The Netherlands receiving honour

indicators.note: receiving means taking in, so the country code holds the other piece inside it

parts.note: NL is the international code for the Netherlands
the OBE, Order of the British Empire, is a British honour

explanation.surface: A well-known Dutch benefactor accepts an award.
explanation.walkthrough: The OBE is an honour awarded by the British monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Nobel left his fortune to fund the Nobel Prizes, making him a renowned benefactor.

clue.text: Author briefly encapsulating first person in intertwined strands

indicators.note: to encapsulate is to enclose as in a capsule, so one piece sits inside
briefly means cut short, so the name loses its final letter

parts.note: Plato, the Greek philosopher and author of the dialogues
I is the first person pronoun

explanation.surface: A writer's short piece wraps a first-person narrator in interwoven storylines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First person' reads as a narrative mode but just supplies the pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: A plait is a braid made by weaving three or more strands of hair or rope together.

clue.text: Weird corona that's seen by Americans at night

definitions.text: that's seen by Americans at night

indicators.note: something weird is strange and out of its normal form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A strange halo in the night sky is spotted over the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a solar or lunar corona; the definition is a nocturnal North American animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Racoons are nocturnal mammals native to North America, so they are what Americans see after dark.

clue.text: Gamble represented giving priority to adult accomplice's role

indicators.note: giving something priority puts it first, so that letter is taken from its place and set at the front

parts.note: a bet is a gamble or wager
to represent something is to mean or signify it
standard abbreviation for adult, as in film ratings

explanation.surface: A wager stood for putting grown-ups first.
explanation.walkthrough: BET followed by MEANT has its A, the adult, moved out of MEANT to the very front.
explanation.definitionFit: Abetment is the act of helping or encouraging a crime, exactly what an accomplice does.

clue.text: Pin dubious statement on bias

indicators.note: in an across clue, putting one thing on another places it after, so the statement follows the bias

parts.note: a skew is a slant or bias
er is the hesitant noise of someone unsure

explanation.surface: Someone blames a misleading claim on prejudice.
explanation.definitionFit: A skewer is a long pin used to hold meat together while cooking.

clue.text: Clubs put forward additional means of attack

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
to lay a proposal is to put it forward
more means additional or extra

explanation.surface: A golfer's or fighter's clubs are presented as an extra weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' sounds like a weapon itself, which fits the attack, but it is just the card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: A claymore is a large two-edged Scottish broadsword, a weapon used to attack.
